utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, I believe you were questioning Mr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. If we could have Mr. Mujadzic recalled to the stand, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have missed you, lawyers. We have been busy in doing other things, but we are happy to be back to see you! MR. MIRSAD MUJADZIC, recalled Examined by MR. KEEGAN, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated, Mr. Mujadzic. You understand you are still under oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mujadzic, since we have had a four-and-a-half day break since you began your testimony, if we might quickly summarise the evidence you have given so far? When we adjourned on Friday afternoon, you had described the ethnic make up and the relations between the ethnic groups in the opstina Prijedor from approximately World War II to about 1990. You stated that Prijedor was considered a model for ethnic relations in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also talked about the rise of Milosevic and his programme to shift the balance of power in the former Yugoslavia to Serbia. You testified that his primary methods to obtain control were the use of propaganda and political manoeuvres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Finally, you also testified about the polarising effect of this political fighting and propaganda on the population in Prijedor and elsewhere, and that it was against this background that the various political parties were founded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You had mentioned briefly the formation of the SDA and its platform. Could you now explain to the court who controlled most of the positions of power in Prijedor prior to the elections of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most positions of power were held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did this apply to positions in the opstina administration, police and the social economy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it can be said, generally speaking, that about 90 per cent of positions in the administration, in social and public enterprises, that 90 per cent of positions were held by Serbs; whereas in the case of private ownership in private companies 90 per cent of the owners were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, what was the platform of the SDS party when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The platform of SDS when it was founded was democracy, protection of the Serb people -- protection of the positions of the Serb people, to be more accurate -- absolute support for Yugoslavia without any reservation and, of course, the support for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you talk about the absolute support for Yugoslavia, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have in mind the proclaimed idea, idea proclaimed by Milosevic, that is, the kind of Yugoslavia that Milosevic presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What is that kind of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a Yugoslavia in which the Serbs would dominate, in other words, greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When you talk about protection for the positions of the Serb people, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned that the Serbs held 90 per cent of the positions in the state owned and public sector or social sector. Actually, SDS was intended to protect the position of the Serbs holding these posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What about the other main party in Bosnia, the HDZ, what was its platform when it was formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The platform of HDZ was also democracy, protection of the rights and interests of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including religious rights, cultural rights, but within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How would you describe the relations between the three main political parties, when they were founded in 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those relations among the political parties were similar to those existing among the people. I mentioned earlier on that two blocks had been formed; the block for the Milosevic type Yugoslavia, in other words, a greater Serbia, and a block against Milosevic's Yugoslavia or, rather, greater Serbia. So that, at first, relationships between SDA and HDZ were normal; whereas there were problems with SDS virtually from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the basis for the SDA's relations with other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no special programme, nor did we receive any special instructions from our headquarters. The basis of relations was contained in the programme of the party, that is, democracy, respect of human rights, respect of the rights of others, to religious and national affiliations and all other human rights that this implies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What efforts, if any, did you make to work together with the other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were some of those efforts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even before the elections, we tried several kinds of co-operation with other parties. In view of the national makeup or the ethnic makeup, we paid special attention to relations with the SDS. So that we proposed to them that we launch a joint election campaign in the sense of joint appearances on the radio and on television, joint election marketing campaigns and joint electoral meetings in communities with mixed populations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you hold any joint rallies or meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I emphasise that all initiatives for co-operation came from our side. In the village of Orlovci, the one and only joint rally was held which is a mixed environment, but the Serbs have a majority, and at the rally attended mostly by Serbs Mevludin Semenovic spoke, who was at the time a candidate for the council of municipalities, the SDA candidate. However, later we learnt that the local SDS leadership from Orlovci was severely criticised by the communal committee of SDS because of this proposal, and after that there were no joint rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What other methods of joint campaigning did you propose to the other two parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a proposal on a joint poster, election poster, which was sent to all the parties, that is HDZ and SDS and others, because the message was a general message.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that message on the placard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The placard said: "We lived and we will continue to live together", and that was the slogan with which we meant that life under new democratic relations and given the changes we aspired to in the sense of inter-ethnic tolerance and good relations is possible even without the communist limitations that we had before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the placard look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our intention was with this placard to express our desire for communality and good relations among all three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the proposal for the placard we had symbols of all three peoples or, rather, the flags of all three peoples. In the middle was the Serb symbol and on each side the symbols of Croatia and the Muslims, the Muslim national symbol.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did the HDZ and SDS respond to this proposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HDZ accepted the placard and they posted it in Croatian communities because, at least as far as Prijedor is concerned, I am quite confident that they had accepted the idea of togetherness, whereas SDS accepted it verbally, but they did not wish to post it in Serb environments, and where the communities were ethnically mixed, where the Muslims posted this placard, their activists tore them down. It is worth noting a commentary made by a member of the communal committee of SDS, Stojan Vracar; he raised the question at a meeting of the communal board of SDS, how could you possibly imagine that Serb symbols and signs should stand between the Ustasha and the Turk symbols?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did the SDS present itself to the other parties and the population at large as the elections drew closer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the election campaign and in their public statements, at public rallies, on the radio, in the press, in their marketing materials, they did not conceal the fact that they were consistently following the policies of Milosevic. However, at their meetings in ethnically pure Serb communities, they went a step further. At those rallies from the very beginning nationalist and chauvinist songs were sung, spreading dissent and hatred for non-Serbs. There are several typical songs or slogans and, if necessary, I can cite them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have conversations with party leaders, the SDS party leaders, about the positions and public statements that were occurring at these rallies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions, both officially and informally, we cautioned the leadership of SDS about such incidents. I personally spoke a couple of times with the President of SDS, Srdjo Srdic, but each time the answer was that this was not their official policy, or their official positions, and that these were irresponsible individuals. When we said that there were too many such irresponsible individuals, he answered: "Do not worry, we have them all under control".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there any change in the statements as the elections drew nearer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for the worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: When were the elections held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: November 18th 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: These were the first democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What positions were up for election on the ballots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the elections we were voting for delegates to the Republican parliament and for delegates to the communal parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the composition of the opstina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The municipal parliament in Prijedor had a total of 90 seats, and the Prijedor opstina, unlike all other opstinas throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, was divided into five electoral units or constituencies, and each party had a total of 90 candidates on the ballot paper and, of course, it was obtained, the number of seats, depending on the votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the composition of the Republic Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Republic Assembly was composed of two chambers, the chamber of the citizens and the chamber of municipalities or opstinas, so that there were two different ballot papers for the Republic parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How were the candidates listed for the council of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the council of municipalities, there were a total of 110 seats in the Republic Assembly, because on behalf of each municipality only one candidate was elected since in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a total of 110 municipalities and that is equal to the 110 seats. However, on each ballot paper there was only one name attached to each party. In our particular case, the municipality of Prijedor, candidates were given by SDA, SDS and the opposition block. Therefore, on the ballot paper for the council of municipalities there was a total of three names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mevludin Semenovic was the candidate for SDA and, in fact, was the person elected to that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the SDA candidate was elected on behalf of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the council of citizens, how were the candidates represented on that ballot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the council of citizens, the electoral system was different. Bosnia-Herzegovina is divided into seven regional constituencies. Those were Bihac, Banja Luka, Doboj, Tuzla, Zenica, Sarajevo and Mostar. Each regional constituency had the right to provide the number of deputies proportionate to the number of voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For Banja Luka how many candidates were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For Banja Luka, the number was 25 candidates and each party at the level of the region proposed 25 candidates, but on the ballot paper itself only the leaders of entire lists were named, and not all the members of the list. So that each party received the number of seats according to the number of votes it won going according to the order of the names listed from (1) down the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In that election in November 1990 for the council of citizens, how many seats did the SDA win for the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the regional level, the number was 13 for SDS, five deputies for SDA, three deputies for HDZ, and I think four for the opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Whose name was represented for the SDA on that ballot for the council of citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDS -- are you asking me for the name for SDS or SDA?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For SDA, my name figured on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: For the opstina Assembly, what were the results of the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the opstina level, SDA had the best result with 30 deputy seats, followed by SDS with 28 seats, HDZ, two seats and 30 seats for the opposition party, the Social Democratic Party, the Liberal Alliance, and the Reform forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did those results mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As in any democratic election, SDA as the winning party had the right to elect first, to be first to elect positions, and to form a government at the level of the opstina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did that mean, "to form a government at the opstina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It meant that some key positions in the opstina would have to be elected by the Assembly which, of course, implied a constituent session of the opstina Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who would have first choice in appointing positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The right to first choice was according to the electoral results enjoyed, of course, by SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Under the results who would the SDA normally choose for partners in the coalition to form a majority government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the basis of the results of the election, if all parties were to be counted, then SDA would have had to get a third of the seats, SDS less than one-third, HDZ a small percentage, a small share, and the opposition as a whole one-third. If the opposition was not counted or was excluded, then of course the relationships would be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What decision was reached on what partners would form the coalition for the opstina government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We offered, first, that we were joined by the opposition in a coalition, because it seemed to us that their reasoning was far sounder and better which, of course, was our electoral right. However, SDS opposed this very strongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So where was the decision finally made -- at the opstina or the Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our next proposal was that SDS should join in forming the government, and that this should be a government constituted by all parties. However, at the Republic level a decision was taken among the leaderships of the three parties at the Republic level, that opposition parties not be included in the formation of the government and that only SDA, SDS and HDZ participate in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: So based on the results in Prijedor, as you previously mentioned them, that would result in the SDA having 50 per cent of the appointed positions with the SDS and the HDZ making up the other 50 per cent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. If we were to respect the results of the elections, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was that, in fact, the case? Is that the agreement that was reached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because SDS did not want to respect the results of the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did the SDS want?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDS wanted to have at least 50 per cent for itself alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there similar problems going on in other opstinas in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the SDS had not won a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but I cannot hear the interpretation now. I speak English and I can understand your question, but would the interpretation into Bosnian switch on, please, because I would not like any confusion to arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Shall I repeat the question? Were there similar problems going on in other opstinas in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the SDS had not won a majority in the election?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina there were similar problems, but it was particularly felt in Prijedor. Generally speaking, one might say that almost in all municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina where SDA had the majority, they gave the SDS more than warranted by election results; and where SDS had the majority and SDA was the minority, the SDA got less than warranted by election results and in some cases it did not even participate in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the same period you were also involved in the establishment of the Republic Assembly and its functions and committees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How well was the Republic Assembly functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost from the very beginning, from the first session problems began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were some of those problems at the very first session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the problem was in the oath of allegiance. Before we took the oath, that is, before the parliament was constituted, SDS opposed the text of the oath because it began with Bosnia-Herzegovina and then Yugoslavia which was only logical since it was the Republic parliament. They insisted that Yugoslavia be placed the first in the oath of allegiance which was unusual and illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were some of the major problems that developed in the initial meetings of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember if it was the first or the second parliament, but the problem about the extension of the law on an additional tax levied in favour of the Yugoslav People's Army arose at that already, and I think at the third or the fourth session problem with the Federal budget began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the problem with the additional tax for the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In point of fact, it was a provisional law and its validity was to be extended because it was about to expire. HDZ was against that law explicitly. We were against it, but we wanted some of our comments to be adopted which would make the law acceptable to us and SDS was urging its adoption or, rather, the extension of its validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What were the main objections to allowing the additional tax for the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our principal objection could be reduced to saying that the Yugoslav People's Army at that time already was less and less Yugoslav and less and less people's and increasingly Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there some particular actions the JNA had recently taken that prompted the refusal to support this tax?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the eve of the elections, several quite significant moves of the chiefs of staff or, rather, the leadership of the Yugoslav People's Army happened and those were initiated by the Federal leadership of the army; that was the attitude of the army towards the Republican Territorial Defence and the Territorial Defence which until that time fell under the jurisdiction of the Republican authorities was now placed under the direct control of the Yugoslav Army itself. Then from the depots of armaments for the Territorial Defence, the weapons were transferred and stored in the JNA depots and it happened throughout Yugoslavia almost with the exception of Slovenia. So the Slovenians interfered and prevented the section of the Yugoslav People's Army early on. Then the changes which happened immediately before the elections in the organisation of the Yugoslavia People's Army; like any other army, the organisation of the Yugoslav People's Army was based principally on the communication, strategic considerations and perceived Yugoslavia as a whole, but it also respected political specificities of the former Yugoslavia. The former Yugoslavia was divided into five army districts, Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade, Skopje and Sarajevo, called after the capitals of individual republics. Army districts largely overlapped, not completely, but by and large overlapped, with the Republican boundaries. The army organisation abolished the Sarajevo army district, and Bosnia-Herzegovina was reduced to a lower organisational level, to a corps. Then a very telling process which had begun to develop earlier on in the army, that is, both the quality and quantity of non-Serb personnel began to decrease. In Tito's time, for instance, there were always four to six generals who were Muslims, then so many Slovenians, so many Croats and other peoples which in a manner guaranteed, was a guarantee, that this was the army of all the peoples. On the eve of the elections, there was no Muslim general in the Yugoslav People's Army, as far as I know, and the number of Croats and other peoples in important positions had already declined significantly and the number of Serbs significantly rose. Finally, it is important to mention that the Yugoslav political army had made its political option as it is established, and this began with the highest ranking army officers by founding the League of Communist movement for Yugoslavia which, in fact, endorsed the idea of unitary Yugoslavia, in other words, the idea of Milosevic's Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were also budget problems related to the Federal budget. What were the nature of those problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the wake of the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia and Croatia began little by little to pay less and less taxes into the Federal budget, so that practically only Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro were paying into the Federal budget, because Macedonia had also announced already that it would not be paying the taxes meant for the Federal budget; whereas the question of the new organisation of the new -- until the, pending, that is, dissolution of the reorganisation or the new organisation of Yugoslavia. Our proposal was not to deny the tax for the Federal budget, but to open a special account for this budget until the solution of the problem of the organisation of Yugoslavia and, therefore, the share in the Federal budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was this proposal accepted by the SDS members of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SDS was categorical in demanding that Federal taxes continued to be paid into the Federal budget. It was absolutely illogical to our minds that their interests were evidently directed more at Belgrade than their own Republic, that is, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: After these initial Assembly meetings, what did you see for the future of a government in the Republic with all three main parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even before the new year, that is, after some three or four sessions of the Assembly -- I am referring to the new year of 1990 -- I was discussing a matter with a fellow deputy and we noted that the relations were deteriorating from one session to the other and increasingly conducive to separation or, rather, a split. We realised that if SDS continued along that road that it would probably result in a war, since intransigent political attitudes under the circumstances could not but result in a war, and it seemed that the SDS or, rather, that the politics pursued by the SDS was in preparation for a long time and that they would not renounce their views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During this time period -- we are talking now November and December 1990 -- was the issue of the establishment of the opstina government in Prijedor still a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Had you met with the opstina SDS leaders to try to resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more than 10 times and with no success, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the main obstacle this issue of the having at least 50 per cent of the appointed positions and control in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the principal obstacle and which we feared was the disrespect for the election results by the SDS who simply could not come to terms with the fact that it was a party which was to get less than 50 per cent according to the election results. However, during the negotiations we tried to arrive at a compromise, and offered some concessions to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were they accepted by the opstina members of the SDS at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regrettably, they did not accept these concessions. They insisted emphatically and would not give up those 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you then meet with Radovan Karadzic and members of the Prijedor SDS in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it happened by accident. It was not a previously organised deliberate meeting. It happened, namely, during the intermission of a parliamentary session. Jovo Tintor, a close associate of Radovan Karadzic, invited me to the hall, to the lobby, of the parliament. When I came, there was Radovan Karadzic and Srdjo Srdic, President of the Prijedor municipal SDS committee, were sitting at a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did Srdic say were the demands of the Prijedor SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He first accused the SDA of endangering the interests of the Serb people in Prijedor, said that no agreement could be reached with us and that our proposals were invariably unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you respond?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I explained in front of Karadzic that our proposal was really tantamount to a concession and that it was a compromise. We proposed 50-50 per cent relationship, that is, 50 per cent for the SDS and 50 for the SDA, and this was per se a concession, and then that each of the parties, "You should give us more percentage for HDZ, in agreement with the electoral results of HDZ which had two seats in Prijedor".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did Srdic react to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He got very angry. He was furious. He said: "Do you really think we would permit that an Ustasha Muslim coalition gains control over Prijedor?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did Karadzic say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karadzic was quiet and tried to be nice. He said, he turned to me and said: "Well, try to reach an understanding and be good to my Serbs, do not threaten them and do not make them angry because they can be very disagreeable when they get angry". Even though he said it with a very polite face, it obviously sounded like a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you reach a compromise at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I then accepted, agreed finally, to meet the SDS request and make yet another concession to give them a 50 per cent, and that we should give HDZ a certain number, a certain proportion, out of our share alone. I accepted this proposal in principle, saying that I would have to consult my municipal leadership and the Republican leadership about this attitude, wishing to reach a compromise and find, devise some ways and means of maintaining good relations with the Serbs, and in this I was supported by both the municipal and the Republican leadership for these concessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How was this compromise implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was implemented at the constituent Assembly of the municipal hall which took place in the beginning of January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were there any people from outside of the opstina taking part in that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Velibor Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic is a member of the leadership of the Serb Democratic Party, one of the closest, confidential Karadzic's men, and at that time he was acting as the Minister for Information in the Government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Why was he at the Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the municipal, SDS leadership was severely criticised by the Republican SDS leadership for losing the elections in Prijedor. In the eyes of the Republican SDS, the municipal SDS should have won the elections in Prijedor and in many other places, indeed, where the ratio between the Muslims and the Serbs, and even where the Muslims' share was five or six per cent as, for instance, in Sanski Most where there are five or six per cent more Muslims than Serbs, and yet the SDS won the elections. So, evidently, Karadzic was showing that he did not trust the opstina leadership, their ability, their ability to reach a compromise in the implementation of the agreement. Ostojic was evidently there to back the opstina leadership and mediate in the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the agreement implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What positions were selected for the opstina administration and filled at that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the main positions in the municipality, the Mayor of the municipality, the President of the municipal government, Deputy Mayor and Deputy President of the opstina government, and eight municipal ministerial posts -- well, as a matter of fact, there were secretaries there, municipal secretaries, holding individual offices in the municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was selected as the President of the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The President of the municipal government became Mico Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could I have photograph 5/107 on the computer screen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What exhibit is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe that is Exhibit No. 138. I am sorry. It would be 137. It has been marked. (To the witness): Do you recognise that picture, the man on the left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mico Kovacevic, Milan, Mico Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the man who was elected as the President of the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I would tender Exhibit 137, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to 137?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Who was selected as the Mayor of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professor Muhamed Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was he the nominee from the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who was selected as the Deputy Mayor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could I have photograph 5/106, please, on the computer? That would be Exhibit No. 138. (To the witness): Do you recognise that picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I would tender Exhibit 138, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 138 will be admitted. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): What other appointed positions in the opstina government were discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the positions in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was the system for the appointments in the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the party which had won the elections, we were entitled to submit our proposal to the Minister of the Interior for the first post in the police, that is, the chief of the police. We did submit our proposal, and our nominee was appointed by the Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who was the SDA nominee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In fact, did he take up this position as the police chief?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Who was entitled to appoint the second position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Deputy Chief of the police or, rather, the post of the Commander of the police was to be proposed by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was the nomination accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS nominated inadequate persons in terms of their educational levels, because any candidate for that post was to have graduated, was supposed to have a university degree, and the SDS nominated a candidate who only had completed secondary school, so that their candidates simply were not adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What did the Ministry of the Interior decide for that Deputy position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Ministry left in that position the former Commander of the police, that is, the person who performed that duty before the elections, until such time when the SDS would submit a proposal that would meet the terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What effect did that have on the negotiations for the remaining positions of the sector chiefs or section chiefs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Namely, in the police, in addition to these two posts first, ranking posts, there were six important officers more, I mean leading executive posts, and they were all taken by Serbs. We requested that a certain ethnic balance be struck within the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What was the SDS position on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDS did not go along with that. They asked us to prevail upon the Minister of the Interior, to appoint their candidate who did not meet the conditions, to appoint him to the office of the chief of the police and, in return, they would enable us to have a man in one of these six positions. This, we could not accept for two reasons: first, because we could not prevail upon the Minister to do something in transgression of the law, anything that would be wrongful and, secondly, because their proposal was not acceptable. It would have been logical that at least two of these six posts available be ceded to non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were there other positions in the financial, industrial and economic sectors of the opstina that you also wanted to negotiate over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we wanted in other areas, in other walks of life, such as socially owned and private companies and other institutions of importance, we wanted to have a balance in them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In terms of the financial, economic and the public, industrial positions, how successful were these discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said about 90 per cent of the positions in financial institutions, in social and public enterprises were held by Serbs. The SDS acted as a protector, as a patron, of all of them and did not want to take part in the balloting of these positions or, rather, they wanted to maintain the previous state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Why were these positions, these appointments, so important?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is simply that we wanted in this manner to strike a balance between the political, economic power at the municipal level and the SDS wanted to keep complete control for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Once the opstina administration was established, what other significant problems or crises did you face in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the course of 1991 there were several critical points. The first occurred after the population census in 1991, and then the SDS leadership wanted to open the discussion again about the post of the Secretary for Defence, that is, they wanted that position for themselves, even though there was already an SDA candidate appointed. There was also a crisis concerning the drafting for the Yugoslav People's Army after the war broke out in Croatia. Then there were problems with drafting lists which the Yugoslav People's Army wanted to take over from the Secretariat for Defence and put them under its control. There was a problem regarding the transit of a large armoured unit from Serbia via Prijedor. It was stationed at the Urije airfield for a while. Then I might mention some important moments, such as the establishment of the Serb autonomous region, Karadzic's statement in the parliament. In the meantime, I had another contact with Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You mentioned first the population census of 1991. What problems did those results cause?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The previous population census of 1981 showed the population structure to be as follows: 43 per cent were Serbs, 38 per cent were Muslims, Croats about six per cent, and the rest were Yugoslavs and others. But it is important to compare the 1981 census and the 1991 census, because the population of 1981 showed that there were five per cent more Serbs than Muslims and the 1991 census showed the ratio to have reversed. So, that the Muslims became the majority in the Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What reaction did that cause among the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In absolute figures, in Prijedor there were 49,700 Muslims and about 48,000 Serbs, and that is about 1,700 Muslims more than the Serbs. There was a characteristic reaction of a member of the municipal SDS leadership who upon learning about the results said: "Give me an automatic rifle and in a couple of hours I will turn this result in the favour of Serbs by killing some 2 to 3,000 Muslims." That member of the municipal leadership came from Omarska. I do not remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You indicated that the call for mobilization when the war in Croatia started also caused significant problems in the opstina. What were the nature of those problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Namely, in the beginning of the war in Croatia, the Yugoslav People's Army proclaimed the mobilization. We acted in conformity with the instruction of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, advising the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to respond in favour of military mobilization because we did not want to take part in an aggression, in the aggression, against the neighbouring Croatia. So that we advised the citizens of Prijedor not to accept, not to agree to be called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There were, in fact, groups who mobilized in opstina Prijedor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a certain number of Serbs did respond favourably to mobilization.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In any of those mobilization calls in the Prijedor opstina, were there some incidents involving non-Serbs that caused concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor, the mobilization took place so that two brigades were founded and reinforced. I think they were the 5th Kozara and the 43rd Brigade, I think. There was a characteristic example when the 5th Kozara Brigade was formed, and that was the TO Brigade. Its Commander was Pero Colic, Colonel Pero Colic. When the citizens received summonses and accepted to be mobilized into that Brigade, it became members of that Brigade. Then in Jaruge, which is a place in the municipality of Prijedor where that unit had its meeting point, then those men who came there, by and large, did not know what was the purpose of the call up and where they were supposed to go. When they heard that immediately after the forming of brigades they were to go to Croatia, they began to protest. Then Colonel Colic stood up and said or, rather, delivered a nationalistic, chauvinistic speech and said as follows -- I am paraphrasing -- "Those who want to follow me in the defence of Serbhood which is endangered in this historical hour, and those who want and understand that an historic time has come when the Serb people needs to take vengeance, to avenge all the crimes committed against them, and to prevent that the Ustase cannot, Ustasha never kills the innocent again, those should come to this side; those who do not want that should move to the other side". After those words, people separated. The Serbs remained on one side; on the other side remained non-Serbs as well as a considerable number of Serbs. Amongst this group which was for Colic, there were a number of men who wore Chetnik insignia which annoyed, which vexed the non-Serbs. So that from the group which followed, which sided with Colic, they began verbally attacking those Serbs who had joined the other side in the sense of threats, such as "traitors", how the Serb people, "you will pay when we come back from Croatia", "cowards". After that, some Serbs changed their mind and joined Colic from that group which was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might that be a good time to break?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question before we recess: Mr. Mujadzic, you testified a few questions back that, "We did not respond favourably to the mobilization call because we did not want to fight against Croatia". Who was the "we"? Was that the SDA party or was that a particular ethnic group that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the differentiation or, rather, the said division into two groups, for Milosevic's Yugoslavia, that is, for Milosevic's Serbia, greater Serbia, rather, that it found its reflection there, in the mobilization. The mobilization call was responded to favourably by the Serb population mostly, that is, over 95 per cent, and all non-Serbs did not refuse the mobilization, including Muslims, Croats and many others who defined themselves as Yugoslavs, as Bosnians and various other ethnic groups which were quite numerous in Prijedor. So that once again there was a split, a schism, between the two blocks that I have been talking all this time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think I know the answer. It must have been this SDA party he was talking about; maybe we will locate it in the transcript ---

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I believe you stated that the initiation for this refusal for the call for mobilization came from an order of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was then issued out to all of the opstinas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Karadzic were the official authority of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, may I just ask a question of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. THE PRESIDING JUDGE (To the witness): Before we recessed, I had asked you about a response that you had made to a question from Mr. Keegan. It really was just to get an understanding of whom you were referring to when you mentioned "we acted". So let me read the question back again and then see if you can respond. The question was from Mr. Keegan: "You indicated that the call for mobilization when the war in Croatia started also caused significant problems in the opstina. What were the nature of those problems?" Then your answer, sir, was: "Namely, in the beginning of the war in Croatia, the Yugoslav People's Army proclaimed the mobilization. We acted in conformity with the instruction of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and advising the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to respond in favour of mobilization because we did not want to take part in an aggression, in the aggression, against the neighbouring Croatia. So that we advised the citizens of Prijedor not to accept, not to agree, to be called up". So my question is, who is the "we"? Who do you mean when you say "we"? Would you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this specific case when I said "we", I can speak only in my own name or in the name of the SDA party of which I was the President in Prijedor. That was our reaction. But an identical reaction was shown by all other parties and political associations except the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, you said earlier when you were listing out the various problems or crises for 1991, you mentioned that in the context of this mobilization conflict there was also some problems related to the position of the Secretary for Defence in the opstina. Can you describe what the problem was with relation to that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. The translation is "Deputy Secretary". Was the question asked in reference to the Deputy Secretary of Defence in the opstina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: No, the Secretary or Minister of Defence for the opstina. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were talking about the position of the Secretary for Defence who, according to the original agreement, was held by a representative of SDA -- Becir Medunjanin is his name. The Serbs or, rather, SDS suddenly raised again the question of this position. This happened before the mobilization and before the request of the Yugoslav People's Army for these mobilization lists, and at first we did not quite understand why they insisted on raising this question again, and why suddenly they were so eager to get that post. We thought that in this way they wanted to cause a problem over the other unappointed positions in financial institutions and enterprises. However, later it became clear to us why they started insisting again on having a representative of their party, the SDS, holding this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not agree to this question being raised again and to discussing it all over without having at the same time taken a step forward in achieving a balance in the distribution of the other very important positions in social enterprises, financial institutions and other important sectors, which were mostly held by SDS, so that these negotiations were protracted. Then came the demand of the Yugoslav People's Army for exemption of lists for mobilization and then the problems around mobilization occurred. So that we assumed that that was probably the reason why SDS suddenly insisted on raising, on putting on the agenda again the position of Secretary of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the Secretary of Defence control the list for mobilization?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Secretariat for Defence at the opstina level served, in fact, only as a service which at the request of the army or the Territorial Defence or some other structures according to a precisely defined list of priorities, carried out the conscription; so that, according to this priority, the Yugoslav People's Army came first, then came Territorial Defence, third place was held by the reserve forces of the police and, fourth, by civil defence units. Of course, all lists for filling in all these structures were within the framework of the Secretariat of Defence and under the direct control and within the terms of reference of the Secretary of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was a problem when a large unit of tanks arrived from Serbian Prijedor at the airport. Can you describe what happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was in August, July or August, I cannot remember exactly the date. Suddenly, a group of citizens came, very agitated, and said that a long line of tanks and transporters had passed through the city, APCs, in the direction of Urije, which is a district within the city of Prijedor, actually the region around the sports airport of Prijedor. I took a car and drove to Urije to see what was happening. At Urije, I indeed saw between 20 and 30 tanks and armoured personnel carriers and, among the soldiers and officers present there, I learnt that they had come from the direction of Serbia. I do not exactly remember whether it was Smederevo or Svetozarevo. They had come by rail. When I asked whether they could tell me the reason for such a strong force being stationed in the region of Prijedor, they said that -- and added that the people were very upset about it -- they told me that they were not competent to provide answers, and that the answer can be given by General Uzelac who, according to them, was in charge of the operation. Returning from the airport, I met a car. I thought that that it was carrying one of the responsible officers. I waved and asked them to stop. The car stopped, and a Colonel came out who introduced himself as Colonel Kostic. I learnt later that he was in charge of security in the Banja Luka corps. I had a very sharp discussion with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you ask him about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I introduced myself and said I was a member of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I asked him to tell me why such a strong military force was suddenly being stationed in the territory of the Prijedor opstina as no competent authority had been informed about it beforehand. His reply was that he was not obliged to provide any information to any individuals; that the Yugoslav People's Army can freely move about without -- move about throughout the territory of Yugoslavia without asking anyone for permission, and that he does not intend to provide me with any answer. My response was that he does not have to give any answers to me as an individual, but that at least the Republic parliament should be informed about it. Then he went on to say that no Republic parliament can control the army, that he is only accountable to his superior command and the Chief of Staff in Belgrade. I responded by saying that, according to the law, at the request of the Republic parliament, such information can be given, otherwise this would be an undemocratic state, a military junta, rather like the one they had in Chile, and this certainly would not contribute to the development of democracy which we should all seek to achieve because the army, after all, needs to be under the control of civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were your actions on that day raised at a later time in front of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several days later at the first session of the Assembly I had intended to raise this question. However, before I managed to say anything about this incident, Srdjo Srdic, President of SDS and also Deputy in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina on behalf of SDS, took the floor and presented the event as if I had stopped with my car in front of the line of tanks and was so bold as to stop the tanks (which of course was not the case, but rather as I have just described it), but he wanted in saying this to emphasise my responsibility and my irresponsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You also mentioned as one of the significant events in 1991 the speech of Karadzic before the Republic Assembly which occurred in 1991. Were you present when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I remember very well that very important speech. I forgot to mention in answer to the previous question that the reaction in parliament was divided, and that all the people in parliament responded against Srdjo in parliament. They were indignant because the question of the army and its aggression in Croatia was very topical at the time, and later it emerged that those tanks went to Croatia, in fact. As for Karadzic's speech in parliament, I remember very well his speech which shocked all members of parliament and all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was it about that speech that was so shocking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that parliamentary session there were discussions about taking a stand regarding processes that had already taken place in Slovenia and Croatia, the demands for independence submitted by Slovenia and Croatia. At the Assembly the debate had started on the positions of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, the attitude of Bosnia-Herzegovina towards the possible independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The position of the Croatian Democratic Alliance was absolutely clear. They were expressly against the possibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia, and they gave full support to the processes that were taking place in Slovenia and Croatia -- (no translation).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are having a problem with the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am sorry, it must have been a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why do you not repeat the question, Mr. Keegan, and we will have the answer again and we will see if we get the full English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You were just describing the position of the Croatian delegates in the Republic Assembly with regard to what was taking place in Slovenia and Croatia. If you could now move to what was the response of Dr. Karadzic in his speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me repeat once again, the Croatian Democratic Alliance had opted clearly in favour of supporting the processes which were taking place in Slovenia and Croatia in the sense of the independence of those two states, and their definite stand was that Bosnia-Herzegovina should also go along the same road. Karadzic at the time addressed the Muslims, knowing that the decision depended on the representatives of the Muslims who at that time had still not taken a definite stand even though it appeared that the representatives of the Muslims would also opt in favour of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Karadzic said then: "If you embark upon the road which can easily lead you to hell, the road which Slovenia and Croatia have already embarked upon" -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are hearing you. I apologise, Dr. Mujadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The English? I think we can all hear each other. I do not know whether I should apologise yet, I hope it does not happen, you understand, as a physician, sometimes we have difficulties with technical aspects of things. Mr. Keegan, try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. (To the witness): Dr. Mujadzic, if you could continue with the paraphrase of what Dr. Karadzic said in his speech. So far you have -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is very brief, my paraphrasing of the statement of Dr. Karadzic, so I can repeat it again. "If you embark upon the road which will take you to hell, it is a road that Slovenia and Croatia have already taken, what may happen is that you disappear because the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina has no arms, has no army of its own, and if it continues along this road, it will witness bloodshed and probably disappearance from these parts".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Were the reports of this speech also broadcast on TV in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By tradition, Assembly meetings of Bosnia-Herzegovina are fully telecast in Bosnia-Herzegovina so that what Dr. Karadzic said was addressed more to Muslims as a people, because he emphasised that he was addressing the Muslims, and only indirectly did he wish to point out that the responsibility for this decision was with the representatives of the Muslims in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What impact did this speech have on you and the other members of your party?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Keegan. Let us wait just one moment, if we can. I have been told that everything is working fine now; that actually there was some work being performed on another or at another room where there are some other mechanical devices that are being installed and because of that that was interfering with our reception. I think that they have stopped working on that other location so we should have free access to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, please. MR. KEEGAN (To the witness): If I can, Dr. Mujadzic, the question I asked you just before that last interruption was what impact did the speech of Dr. Karadzic have on you and the other members of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way in which Dr. Karadzic made this statement and the tone sounded threatening, he was very angry, and he seemed to be very serious while he was saying this. We were shocked and, I must admit, frightened as well because we knew that the Yugoslav People's Army was well-correlated with this statement by Radovan Karadzic, and soon after this session -- I am sorry, I am sorry, I apologise, in the course of that session, that is, before his statement, a noteworthy statement was one by Deputy of SDS, Kerovic from Lopari, who addressed provocation in the restaurant of the Holiday Inn Hotel, who said to me: "What do you think? We have the Yugoslav People's army with us, what will you do?" I did not want to respond because the question was, obviously, a provocative one, though I knew that his words were fully in line with reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Each of these events that we have discussed for 1991, what did the total of these events represent to you, what did they indicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these events were indicating day after day, week after week, month after month, the deterioration of relations and this was a process -- and there was a process on the way with some events showing that certain things, certain moves by SDS had been planned. Our impression was that we would always be caught unawares by some action, by some move, by the SDS, because we had to look out for a way out from some problem posed by the SDS all the time, and it was more than obvious that they had planned all their activities very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier the Serb autonomous region of the Krajina. Can you describe for the court what that was, what was the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in September 1991, a certain number of SDS MPs did not attend the session that afternoon. On the news we heard that several Serb autonomous regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina had been proclaimed, the Serb autonomous region of Krajina, the Serb autonomous region of Romanija, the Serb autonomous region of Stara Herzegovina, that is, east Herzegovina; and the principal purpose, the principal intent, behind the establishment of Serb autonomous regions was the separation from the Republic, from the Republican government agencies in Sarajevo, and siding, that is, joining with the Yugoslavia, that is, greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where was the Serb autonomous region of the Krajina centered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area which the SDS had envisaged as the Serb autonomous region of Krajina, Bosanska Krajina, is the area of the Banja Luka region to which they added some other municipalities where the Serbs constituted a marked majority, such as Drvor, Bosanska Grahovo, and Teslic, I believe Teslic was also included. Those were areas where the Serbs were in a majority, although they had also included in that area places like Prijedor, Sanski Most, Jajce, Kotor Varos, I think Krupa was also envisaged even though the Serbs were a minority there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did the opstina Prijedor join the Serb autonomous region of the Krajina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What other opstinas in that region did not join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apart from Prijedor, Bosanski Novi did not join SAO Krajina, Prijedor, Sanski Most, towns in the Sana River valley -- these are the three towns in the Sana valley -- and also the municipalities of Jajce and Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I wonder if I can ask, not the witness, but you a question? What do you mean "did certain regions join"? Was it a voluntary thing? How could you join or refuse to join?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, if you could explain, how did opstinas become members of the autonomous region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the SDS leadership had prepared an outline framework to include all the municipalities, but various municipalities, as I have already said, did not become part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did it require ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The admission to the SAO was to be confirmed by the Municipal Assembly, and in the places I have just mentioned the Municipal Assemblies did not vote for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What later happened to each of those opstinas which did not vote to join the autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In these municipalities the most horrendous crimes of ethnic cleansing took place in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Dr. Karadzic about the opstina Prijedor joining the Serb autonomous region of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not any special meeting, and the second meeting with Dr. Radovan Karadzic also took place during a break in the parliamentary session in Sarajevo. I cannot remember who that was, but I know that one of the persons escorting him came to me and asked me to join him and some other SDS members at a table. I do not remember who those others were. Radovan Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic, was in a very good mood and he did his best to be friendly and even cordial. He said: "Listen, you have to know, you have to be aware that the Muslims are, historically speaking, closer to the Serbs than the Croats and you, the Muslims, should be in alliance with Serbs rather than Croats. If the Serbs and the Muslims had an alliance, then we would be able to liberate the whole coast in a very short time, come out to the Adriatic Sea and we could perhaps grant some autonomy to Dubrovnik".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did you respond to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I answer, may I recount another part of his speech, of Dr. Karadzic's speech, which is based upon Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked: "Well, and what are you doing down there in Prijedor? Why do you not join Banja Luka? Prijedor has always been with Banja Luka and not with Bihac". Meanwhile, this group was joined by one of SDA members of parliament, I think it was Zijad Kadic, and he asked him something, I think, if he had heard a part of a speech about a possible alliance between the Muslims and the Serbs and what would be the Muslims' position in that state, in some Yugoslavia; and Karadzic responded that the position of the Muslims would be very good, and that it would be the second people in terms of its size. Then I asked him whether we would have the right to define ourselves as a people, as Bosniaks, for instance. He said: "Why that? Is it not enough for you to be able to define yourself from the point of view of your religion and to cultivate your culture?" So that he did not mention specifically our right to define ourselves ethnically. I listened to him carefully and I told him that we, the Bosniaks, did not opt for an alliance with the Croats, and that we simply had our own road, and that Bosnia-Herzegovina needed to and could survive only as a community of three equitable peoples, Serbs, Muslims and Croats; and that the relations between Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Republic, as a state, with Croatia or Serbia, could only be on an equitable footing balanced, we called it the thesis of equidistance, that is, the same distance kept between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, as this was the only way in which we could achieve stability and solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In reference to Prijedor, I said that it was quite true that, economically speaking, Prijedor had always been linked to Banja Luka but that, politically speaking, we did not want to opt either for Banja Luka or for Bihac, that we simply wanted Prijedor to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What, in fact, was the view of the SDA party on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That view was proclaimed rather in early days during the election campaign at a big rally in Velika Kladusa, and could be summed up as follows -- I am sorry -- if only Slovenia leaves Yugoslavia and Croatia remains in it, then it is still Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina can remain in such Yugoslavia; and if Croatia also leaves Yugoslavia, then the balance is disrupted and this is not Yugoslavia any more, and then we shall have no other choice but to also leave and request the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this view is based on the equidistance thesis, that is, the same distance between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, as Bosnia-Herzegovina could not remain with Serbia if Croatia has separated, has left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was this position of the SDA known to members of the SDS during those early days in the campaign?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this position was stated publicly and this position, this stand, was maintained for one reason and one only, that Bosnia-Herzegovina, this was the only way in which Bosnia-Herzegovina could survive, that this was the only way to preserve its political stability and Bosnia-Herzegovina as one whole, as an entity. That was why we proclaimed that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: With all of these events and situations as the background, how did the Serb referendum or plebiscite and the Bosnia-Herzegovina referendum later on fit into this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb plebiscite is nothing but a point or, rather, the ultimate stage of a process whereby the Serbs, in fact, said "yes" to greater Serbia, said "yes" to Yugoslavia as conceived by Milosevic. So this was the final stage of a process which had begun much earlier, long before the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. So the only possible answer, the only possible response, to the Serb plebiscite which was held, if I am correct, in November 1991, was a referendum on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I believe, some time around February 1992 which was also but a final stage of a process and, generally speaking, one may say that neither of these events were a cause but, rather, a consequence and the effect. I should like to emphasise that the nature of the Serb plebiscite found its reflection in the mode of voting, and our objection after the Serb plebiscite was that it had been undemocratic by nature and for two reasons: First, because the voting, the ballot papers, were one kind for Serbs -- I think, I believe they were blue -- and another kind for non-Serbs -- I think they were red, so that it reminded us of some racist methods and, secondly, the outcome of the referendum was 100 per cent for, which is impossible in a normal democratic procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, as we then move into 1992, between January and April 30th 1992, what significant events or meetings occurred to cause you concern for what was about to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe it was sometime in January 1992. Then there was the decision on the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the decision on the referendum, taken by the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the referendum for independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then at the local level the return of Serb brigades from the front in Croatia, after the cease-fire in Croatia; the occupation of the transmitter on the Kozara mountain which was transmitting the TV signal for the Prijedor region by Serb extremists, and then a series of talks we had with Colonel Arsic, Major Radmilo Zeljaja, Simo Miskovic, the newly elected SDS President, Srdja Srdic. Then the occupation of Sanski Most by the 6th Krajina Brigade and the talks with General Talic and Colonel Hasecic. Then the military coup in Prijedor in the night between 29th and 30th April, and the attack on the civilian population in Prijedor by Serb paramilitary formations and the newly proclaimed army of the Republika Srpska on 23rd May, and the meeting, I forgot that, with Stojan Zupljanin, the head of the Regional Police administration for the region of Banja Luka, rather the head of the security service in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: This meeting with the individual you named as Stojan Zupljanin, who called that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting was called at the initiative of the Regional Police administration, the head of the centre for State Security of Banja Luka, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If could I have photograph 5/109 brought up on a computer, please. That would be Exhibit 139. Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who is that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Stojan Zupljanin. I think he has gained weight in the meantime, but I am positive that that is him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender Exhibit 139.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 139 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where was this meeting with Stojan Zupljanin held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting was held in the building of the municipal hall in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the position of Mr. Zupljanin? What was it that he wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As opstina Prijedor did not join the Serb autonomous region of Bosanska Krajina, the police station for the municipality of Prijedor was neither a part, had neither joined the centre for State Security in Banja Luka, apart from the chief of the police in Prijedor and the Chief of Police in Jajce. All over chiefs of police in all other municipalities were Serbs. Zupljanin questioned the functioning, the operation of the police station in Prijedor and said he found it inadmissible that the Prijedor police station communicates with Sarajevo, that this communication had to be stopped and that the Prijedor police station had to be placed under the sole control of the State Security centre in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was the response from the police authorities in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Talundzic, the Chief of Police who was present at the meeting. May I mention only that apart from the Chief of Police and myself, Muhamed Cehajic, the Mayor of the municipality, was also present. The Deputy Mayor, Milomir Stakic, was also there. The then SDS President, Simo Miskovic. Some individuals escorting Stojan Zupljanin who were armed with automatic weapons entered the room with their weapons who did not introduce themselves, so I do not know who they were. So Chief Talundzic and our answer, that is the Mayor's and my answer, was that the police station in Prijedor would remain within the state structure of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it would respect the decisions and orders coming from its centre, but that we had nothing against establishing some kind of co-operation with the State Security centre in Banja Luka. However, the meeting did not last long. Immediately when he came into the room Mr. Zupljanin was very agitated and angry because outside a large crowd had gathered to protest and they were shouting "Bosnia, Bosnia". He looked very angry and he stood up and left the municipal building in protest.
